lineages.name: D'Angelo and Questlove
lineages.why: D'Angelo's Brown Sugar (1995) helped launch the genre and Voodoo (2000) is called its crowning achievement. Recorded live at Electric Lady with Questlove as co-pilot, Voodoo's grooves were built to hang on the back of the beat: play as well as possible, then deliberately insert the glitch.

lineages.name: J Dilla
lineages.why: Questlove credits him with inventing the sound called neo-soul. On the MPC3000 he set straight and swung time against each other — snares nudged forward, kicks and bass lagging — and that feel leaked into Voodoo's live playing.

lineages.name: Pino Palladino
lineages.why: Wrote every bass line on Voodoo on a 1961 P-bass and played them far behind the beat. He heard the backing tracks as the kind of deconstructed, deliberately messed-up rhythm J Dilla would make.

lineages.name: Erykah Badu
lineages.why: Baduizm (1997) set heavier hip-hop beats under organic soul with Ron Carter on bass and The Roots on some tracks. She was a Soulquarian; Mama's Gun (2000) came out of the same Electric Lady sessions.

name: Neo-soul / contemporary R&B

notes.text: Layers are displaced against each other on purpose: in D'Angelo's 'Left and Right' (92 BPM) the guitar/percussion layer and the kick/bass/snare layer sit about 55 ms apart on beats 1 and 3 and about 80 ms on 2 and 4 — 8–12% of a quarter note — so the beat becomes a wide 'bin' rather than a point.

D'Angelo asked Questlove to play 'drunk' and 'as slow and as dusted' as he had ever played, and Pino Palladino to put the bass far behind the beat; the feel came from J Dilla's MPC work, which pulled basslines far behind, let kicks lag and rushed snares.
Programmed versions keep drums unquantised: kick 2–5 ms early, snare 10–20 ms late, 5–20 ms of human offset, ghost notes at 20–30% velocity; Reason's tutorial warns that quantising makes it stiff.

Nearly every chord is extended to a 9th, 11th or 13th — minor 9 and minor 11 above all, since extended minor chords rarely go past the 11th — in close, middle-register Rhodes or Wurlitzer voicings with the root left to the bass.
Atmosphere over resolution: quartal voicings, parallel planing of one shape, and two-chord vamps are as common as functional ii–V–I; chords are treated as colour, not destination.
Played electric bass, not a sub: Palladino wrote Voodoo's bass lines on a 1961 P-bass, taking Stevie Wonder in the choruses and P-Funk in the verses, and sat far behind the beat.

Rhodes and Wurlitzer, electric guitar, played bass, vintage drums — Electric Lady's 1968 Ludwig kit — and strings (Brent Fischer's string intro on Really Love); organic textures over trap drums and 808s.

Russell Elevado recorded and mixed Voodoo on analogue and vintage gear rather than contemporary digital techniques; guides put bus compression at 2–3 dB of gain reduction and the kick low-passed near 200 Hz.

Loudness is measured R&B/Soul as a whole: 11,412 tracks at a −9.6 LUFS median (middle half −11.2 to −8.3), and a separate BS.1770 survey with R&B at −12.6; neo-soul's live, dynamic records are taken to sit toward the quieter end.
Album-oriented rather than single-driven, with long songs and codas: Untitled (How Does It Feel) runs 7:10 in 6/8 and stops mid-word on the last chorus; Voodoo runs 78:54.

Voodoo was cut live with the players face to face and, apart from Untitled, mostly without overdubs, after the band spent 1996–97 jamming and studying funk and soul recordings; Untitled's harmonies are D'Angelo's own overdubbed voice.
Conscious, introspective singer-songwriter lyrics, with women artists unusually prominent.

evidence.inferred: computed by Bench/genres/melody_ranges.py over https://colinraffel.com/projects/lmd/ and https://www.tagtraum.com/msd_genre_datasets.html

notes.text: Melody ranges are measured, not recalled: 416 eight-bar windows from the melody tracks of 72 Lakh MIDI files labelled RnB by tagtraum, each read with the app's own Melodist arithmetic; the range is the 10th to 90th percentile, typical the median. Performed MIDI, so note lengths are as played. The share of chord tones is not measured: the files carry no chords. The label is the dataset's RnB label, which spans soul, Motown, funk and contemporary R&B.

pitfalls.text: Quantising the drums; the feel lives in the displacement, and a quantised beat reads stiff.

Treating 'behind the beat' as random sloppiness; Dilla's shifts were precise adjustments, and Questlove describes playing as perfectly as possible, then inserting the glitch deliberately and consistently.
Driving every progression to a strong cadence; the style prefers vamps, planing and unresolved colour chords.

progressions.text: The extended ii–V–I, the one functional cadence the style uses freely.
The minor-eleven drift, slow and non-resolving.
Parallel planing: one shape slid down a whole step for colour.
Minor-nine chords on i, v and iv, voiced close with inversions.
The two-chord vamp with the Dorian major IV.

evidence.inferred: beatkey.app's ghost-note velocity of 20–30% of the main hit, converted as 20·log10(0.3) = −10.5 dB and 20·log10(0.2) = −14 dB, assuming velocity maps linearly to amplitude
from the cited lengths: On & On 3:45, Really Love 5:44, Untitled (How Does It Feel) 7:10, with Voodoo running 78:54 as an album of long songs
beatkey.app's sections: a 4–8-bar intro, 16-bar verse and 4–8-bar pre-chorus put the first chorus 24–32 bars in; 24 bars at 95 BPM is 61 s, 32 bars at 70 BPM is 110 s

lufs.to's per-track measurements (https://lufs.to/genres and the release pages its genre pages link; 2,544 distinct tracks across 27 genre pages; 'dynamic range' there is defined on https://lufs.to/methodology as peak minus RMS of the whole track, the same quantity MixMeter.crestDB computes) give crest = 5.28 - 0.743 x integrated LUFS (r = -0.88, residual SD 1.36 dB). Applied to this genre's integrated-loudness range -12.6 to -8.3 LUFS (this profile's own mix.lufs.integrated), typical -9.6 LUFS -> 12.4 dB. Pooled across genres, not a crest measurement of this genre; lufs.to's peak may be true peak, so it can read up to ~0.5 dB above a sample-peak crest.

references.title: On & On

summary: Soul and R&B brought back to live, organic playing and album-length songs, mixed with funk, jazz and hip-hop, as against the producer-driven digital R&B of the 1990s. Its grooves lean on extended ninth and eleventh chords on Rhodes and deliberately displaced rhythm — drums and bass hanging behind the beat in the J Dilla-derived 'drunk' pocket of D'Angelo's Voodoo.
